analysis.title: "Here We Go Again": McElligott Warns Levered ETFs Face Massive $35 Billion Dump Into Today's Close
key_insights: Nomura's Charlie McElligott says AI capex/FCF/financing sustainability worries are back after hyperscaler earnings showed weakening core businesses. Weaker free cash flow implies more debt and equity issuance, which adds supply pressure on the stocks.

Alphabet burned cash and sold stock rather than buying it back. Amazon's free cash flow was -$33.5B in the quarter, more than four times worse than consensus, with capex at $77.3B. Amazon borrowed $48B in the quarter.

On Friday Oct 30 the Nasdaq 100 was down 4% and Goldman's AI basket down 4.7%. The equal-weighted S&P was up 1.2% and the S&P ex-AI was on track for its best month since 2022. Nasdaq 100 members had lost more than $1.2T of market cap in October before the session started.

McElligott attributes the equity selling to excess positioning and a gross leverage/risk-management exercise into year-end. Leveraged investors are worried about drawdown timing ahead of comp/bonus season, so there is low tolerance for losses and little incentive to buy mean-reversion.

Long/short hedge funds' rolling one-month beta to the Mag7 was at the 97th percentile of its decade-long history going into earnings. Nomura also saw large upside call buying in megacaps into the prints, for example GOOGL Jan 360 calls (Alphabet near $290 Thursday) and AMZN Nov 265/295 call spreads (Amazon near $223 after hours Thursday, below the lower strike).

Index options skew has not reacted much to the selloff. McElligott gives three reasons: high dispersion with low correlation (9 S&P sectors higher week-to-date and month-to-date against a Mag7 downdraft), de-grossing that keeps index vol low (shorts covered and higher, longs sold and lower), and low net exposure that reduces the need for downside hedges.

QQQ front-month ATM implied vol jumped more than five points from Thursday's close to about 26.6, above last week's level, with the curve inverted. QQQ wings are bid on the week on hyperscaler capex worries, while SPX stays calm with no real tail-hedge demand.

Treasuries are not rallying further despite the renewed AI capex wobble, which would normally add weight to the economic left-tail scenario for 2027/28 and support bonds as an equity hedge. McElligott attributes this to P&L management (profit-taking on tactical longs) and CTAs needing three-month windows to turn long from short, which has not yet happened broadly.

The rates options market has flipped from an impulsive squeeze of crowded shorts in bonds/STIRS (which hit CTA trend trades) to receivers/calls-over positioning in vol space. McElligott warns this risks negative convexity/gamma acceleration flows into a further rally, with a 'Spot Up / Vol Up' catalyst for large moves.

Into the close, discretionary equity funds have little left to de-risk, so the risk is mechanical flows from systematic and market-structure forces: real negative gamma from legacy hedges (Nasdaq and single-name tech), synthetic negative gamma from leveraged ETFs, and systematic long equity exposure at the 95th percentile.
Nomura estimates vol-control selling of about $31.1B on a 2% SPX decline and $67.2B on a 3% decline.

Nomura projects a levered ETF end-of-day rebalance of -$34.6B, the third-largest one-day levered ETF sale since 2006, with semis at about -$17.4B and tech at about -$11.6B. Only June 5 (-$51.3B) and June 23 (-$38.1B) were larger. 87% of levered ETF AUM is tech-concentric, out of $168.1B total. The complex has sold $63.4B over the past month, $34B of it in semis.

Aggregate selling including dealer short gamma is projected at about $110B on a 2% SPX close, $177.6B at -3%, $228.5B at -4% and $266.3B at -5%. A 1% rally brings about $47.6B of buying, peaking at about $51.8B at +2% before fading as vol control sells into the rally.

If the S&P closes flattish, the vol-control trigger does not fire and the equal-weight rally can keep masking the damage in AI names. The article's author expects more de-grossing in AI names, more issuance, and eventually a bond rally.

market_movers.rationale: Alphabet burned cash and sold stock instead of buying it back. The shares were back to where they were on this day in 2025, and the Jan 360 calls bought into earnings are far out of the money.

Free cash flow was -$33.5B in the quarter, over four times worse than consensus, on $77.3B of capex. Amazon borrowed $48B in the quarter and traded near $223 after hours Thursday, below the lower strike of the Nov 265/295 call spreads.
Intel was suffering its steepest intraday drop in history on Oct 30.

sector_views.rationale: Semis account for about $17.4B of the projected $34.6B levered ETF rebalance sale and $34B of the $63.4B sold over the past month.
Selling is centered on AI megacap tech and hyperscalers after 1-2 years of large gains, while 9 S&P sectors are higher on the week and month.

risk_factors: Mechanical selling into the close from levered ETFs, vol-control funds and dealer negative gamma.
Year-end de-grossing and drawdown-averse leveraged investors.
Rising debt and equity issuance to fund AI capex, which pressures both stocks and credit spreads.
A bond rally that starts a 'Spot Up / Vol Up' feedback loop in rates.

tension_points.bull_case: The equal-weighted S&P is up 1.2% and the S&P ex-AI is on track for its best month since 2022, with 9 S&P sectors higher on the week and month. A flattish S&P close means the vol-control trigger never fires.
tension_points.bear_case: Levered ETFs (-$34.6B), vol-control funds, dealer negative gamma and 95th percentile systematic exposure sell into weakness. Capex keeps growing while free cash flow shrinks, financed with more debt and equity issuance.
tension_points.what_invalidates: The S&P finishing flattish into the close would keep the vol-control trigger from firing and defuse the mechanical selling.
